member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.IRhiCommandEncoder
member.summary: Records work for the GPU: passes, copies and queries.

remarks.para: One encoder records one submission. It is not thread-safe and is not meant to be: the frame is recorded from one thread, and an implementation is free to write straight into a command buffer.

There are no barriers here. What a resource is ready for is the implementation's business: Vulkan tracks it and inserts the transitions, WebGPU has no such notion at all. A pass that reads what another pass wrote simply reads it, and an implementation that needs a barrier to make that true puts one in. This is the single largest difference from the interface it replaces, and the reason a browser backend is possible.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.IRhiDevice
member.summary: A graphics device, as everything above it needs one: resources, pipelines, a command encoder and a frame to present.

remarks.para: WebGPU's model, because it is the narrower of the two and a narrower interface can be implemented over a wider one. The reverse cannot: a browser cannot be asked for a subpass, a barrier, a descriptor pool or a memory type, while Vulkan can be asked to do without all four.

Nothing here knows what a frame of this game looks like. Which passes run in what order, what the G-buffer holds and when the surface cache is relit belong above, in the shared pipeline, so that both backends draw the same frame rather than two frames that resemble each other.

member.summary: Sends everything submitted so far to the GPU now, and waits until it has finished.

remarks.para: A backend may hold what is submitted during a frame and send it when the frame ends -- the Vulkan one does, so that the image acquired for the frame is waited on once and presented once. That leaves nothing a readback made in the middle of a frame can wait for. This sends the held work ahead of the frame's end, so a readback of what it wrote completes; the frame then goes on and ends as usual.
A diagnostic's tool, not a frame's: it stalls the host on the GPU. Where the platform cannot block, it sends what it holds and returns, and a readback polls across frames instead.

member.summary: NVIDIA's Streamline features, where the device runs them: DLSS, ray reconstruction, frame generation, Reflex.

remarks.para: A capability interface, like : only a Vulkan device that started the optional Streamline runtime has one, and everything that uses it asks and falls back to the engine's own path when the answer is null. It speaks RHI types only — the handles, the formats, the layouts and the command buffer stay inside the backend — so the shared pipeline drives it without knowing which API is underneath.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.RhiFeatures
member.summary: The optional things a device can do, each of which some device cannot.

remarks.para: Every one of these is a real difference between the machines this runs on, not a hypothetical: a browser has no ray query and no timestamp query, MoltenVK reports its own sample counts, and a desktop driver may or may not filter a 32-bit float texture. A pass asks before it uses one and has something to do when the answer is no — that is the rule the whole renderer already follows for hardware ray tracing, and it is the rule that makes a second backend possible at all.
Presence, not preference. Whether a feature that exists should be used is a setting, and settings live above this.

Whether depth may be clamped rather than clipped at the near and far planes, which is what lets a shadow caster behind the light's near plane still cast.
Whether an indirect draw may start at a non-zero instance.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.RhiTextureFormat
member.summary: What one texel holds.

remarks.para: The formats this renderer actually uses, and no others. A longer list would be a list of things a pass could ask for and a backend could not provide: WebGPU's format table is shorter than Vulkan's, its storage-texture support shorter still, and a format offered here that one backend cannot write to is a pass that works on one machine and not the other.

Colour space is part of the format. The sRGB pairs below are not an encoding detail to be applied later: a view created as sRGB has the hardware convert on every read and write, and one created without it does not. Mixing them up is the single most common way for a renderer to come out uniformly washed out or uniformly dark.
